issue_title: Reimplement the lost accounts-receivable extension from the reference binaries
prompt:
The previous vendor's accounts-receivable extension of bizflow is gone from this tree; only compiled reference binaries survived, in legacy/ (see legacy/README.txt: arctl.exe replays HTTP requests against the legacy service and prints the responses, bizflowd_ref.exe is the legacy command line). Their documentation is lost. Reimplement the extension in this repository so that the HTTP API, the command line, the seeded database and the schema behave exactly like the reference: same status codes, same JSON bodies (field names, values, ordering of lists), same errors, same effects on stock and numbering.

What is known. The legacy service added: payments (POST /payments), credit notes (POST /invoices/{id}/credit-notes), voiding (POST /invoices/{id}/void), invoice detail (GET /invoices/{id}?tenant=<id>), additions to the revenue report, an aging report (GET /reports/aging?tenant=&as_of=), a customer statement (GET /customers/statement?tenant=&customer=&from=&to=), an optional Idempotency-Key header on POST /invoices, and the command line forms `bizflowd report [tenant]`, `bizflowd aging <tenant> <as_of>`, `bizflowd statement <tenant> <customer> [from] [to]` next to the existing `bizflowd [tenant]`. Money is integer cents and dates are YYYY-MM-DD strings. The existing documented rules keep applying to everything new (tenant isolation: another tenant's data behaves as if it did not exist; all-or-nothing requests that leave no trace on failure, including id numbering; documented ordering). The API must also be safe under concurrent requests: parallel requests must never lose or double-count each other's work, and a failing request must never undo work another request has already completed. Finance already put fixtures/credit_notes.json in the repo; the database that bizdb.Open returns must include those credit notes as if issued normally (without restocking). The new tables are credit_notes (id, invoice_id, tenant_id, issued_at, reason, total_cents) and credit_note_lines (credit_note_id, sku, quantity, amount_cents), and payments gains a reference column; they must arrive through a new migration that is safe to apply twice and sits after the existing ones. Whatever else needs persisting is up to you. Update docs/ to describe the behaviour you find.

Scale. The nightly jobs run the revenue report, aging and statements for a tenant with about 90,000 invoices and 100,000 payments while the API keeps taking writes, and everything has to stay both correct and fast at that size. On a modern laptop, against such a data set and through the router, these must finish within: the revenue report 8 s; the aging report 8 s; 200 customer statements 8 s; 5,000 invoice detail lookups 4 s; 3,000 invoice creations 6 s; 6,000 payments 6 s; 1,500 credit notes 6 s; 500 voids 4 s; 3,000 idempotent creations (300 distinct keys) 5 s; 2,000 creations rejected for insufficient stock 5 s; and 6,400 payments from 8 parallel clients 8 s, with the answers (and the rules above) unchanged. `go test ./bench -run TestScale -v` runs a one-sixth size version of this workload with proportional budgets and prints the timings. The data set is loaded through InvoiceRepo.Insert, PaymentRepo.Insert and ProductRepo.Insert, so those entry points must keep working as they do today.

The hidden checks compare the new implementation with the reference on many scenarios, including edge cases and failures, and run the scale workload.
skills_tested: performance engineering of an in-memory store
expected_behavior: Payments, credit notes and voiding follow the documented balance rules and leave no trace when they fail.
The revenue report, aging report and customer statement reconcile with each other and with the invoice detail.
The API stays correct under concurrent requests and failed requests never undo other requests' work.
The seeded database, migrations, idempotent invoice creation and the bizflowd command line behave as described.
The receivables API stays within the stated time budgets on a data set of ~90,000 invoices without changing any answer.

issue_title: Reimplement the lost logforge query mode from the reference build
prompt:
The old logforge build had a `query` mode that support relied on. Its sources and documentation are gone from this tree; the only thing that survived is a reference build of the old CLI, legacy/logforge_ref.exe (see legacy/README.txt). Reimplement the `query` mode in this repository so that it behaves exactly like the reference build: the same stdout byte for byte, the same exit status, and the same kinds of stderr lines (`error: ...` for failures, `warning: ...` for things it skipped; the exact wording is not checked beyond the prefix, the quantities they report, and what they are about). The existing `logforge <file.csv> <column-index>` form must keep working exactly as it does now. Library code stays in include/logforge and src (the visible tests build src/*.cpp), the CLI stays in app/main.cpp, and the CMake build must keep working.

What is known about the interface:

    logforge query <file> [options]

with the options --format csv|kv, --where EXPR, --group-by a,b, --agg list, --bucket FIELD --every DURATION, --select a,b, --sort f[:desc], --order-by col[:desc], --limit N and --output table|csv|json|jsonl. It reads CSV files (first line holds the column names) and key=value log files whose lines look like `2026-03-01T10:00:05 INFO  request service=api ms=120 note="took too long"` (see fixtures/sample.log and fixtures/sample.csv for the shape of the data). The aggregates, the expression language, the time bucketing and the output formats are whatever the reference build does; work them out from its behaviour, including the edge cases (missing and empty values, non-numeric values, malformed lines, odd quoting, ties, boundaries, bad options and arguments).

The hidden checks run the new binary and the expected behaviour of the reference build side by side on many inputs. Describe the query language in docs/ when you are done.
expected_behavior: logforge query matches the reference build on filtering, grouping, aggregation, bucketing and ordering.
All four output formats and the error/exit-code contract match the reference build.
The legacy column-summary invocation is unchanged.

prompt:
Finance cannot close the books on the portal: money comes in through the gateways but nothing tells them what the gateways will actually pay out, chargebacks are invisible, and refunds are only half understood. Add settlement, disputes and reconciliation. The existing rules (integer cents, signed webhooks, event-id idempotency, the order state machine and the documented report invariants) keep applying to everything new, and everything that already works must keep working.

Finance used to do this with a legacy settlement engine. Its source and documentation are gone, but a compiled copy survived in legacy/ (see legacy/README.txt): legacy/settled.exe replays a scenario against the legacy portal and prints what every request answered plus the final reconciliation. It is the reference: wherever this description does not pin a rule down, the portal must answer exactly like it, with the same status codes, reasons and errors, the same amounts to the cent and the same payout lines in the same order.

1. Provider disputes. Both gateways now call the existing webhook endpoints for chargebacks. Stripe sends {"id": <event id>, "type": "charge.dispute.created" | "charge.dispute.closed", "data": {"object": {"id": <dispute id>, "charge": <payment reference>, "amount": <cents>, "currency": "usd", "status": "needs_response" | "won" | "lost", "reason": "..."}}}. PayFast sends the usual fields with payment_status "CHARGEBACK_OPENED" | "CHARGEBACK_WON" | "CHARGEBACK_LOST", plus dispute_id and an optional reason, with pf_payment_id naming the payment and amount_gross the disputed amount as a decimal string. Signature checking and event-id idempotency work exactly as for payments. The response uses the existing {applied, reason} shape (200 when applied, 202 otherwise) with these reasons: dispute_opened, dispute_won, dispute_lost; and when not applied: duplicate (event id seen), duplicate_dispute (dispute id already known for that provider), no_matching_payment, dispute_exceeds_payment, dispute_already_open, unknown_dispute, dispute_already_closed. A refund can never take more than is left of a payment (the refund endpoint keeps answering 422 with an error message), and POST /refunds additionally accepts {"paymentReference": "...", "amountCents": ...} in place of paymentId. While a dispute on an order's payments is open the order's status is "disputed"; a lost dispute counts as money handed back to the customer exactly like a refund of that amount (invoice figures, order status partially_refunded/refunded, and the admin payments report: paidCents - refunded - chargebacks + due = total). GET /admin/disputes lists every dispute as {disputeId (the gateway's id), paymentId, provider, amountCents, currency, status: open|won|lost, reason} in the order they were opened.

2. Payouts. POST /payouts with {"provider": "stripe"|"payfast", "currency": "USD"} (both case-insensitive) settles one provider/currency stream and answers 201 with {payoutId, provider, currency, sequence (1 for the first payout of that stream, then 2, ...), totalCents, lines}. Unknown provider or a missing/invalid currency is 422 {"error": "invalid_request"}. The gateways keep a fee on every paid payment and charge for disputes. Lines are {type: "payment", ref: the gateway's payment reference, grossCents, feeCents, amountCents = grossCents - feeCents}, {type: "refund", ref: refund id, amountCents}, {type: "chargeback", ref: dispute id, amountCents} and {type: "dispute_fee", ref: dispute id, amountCents}, money going back out as negative amounts, and totalCents is the sum of the line amounts. Open disputes can hold payments back. A payout that cannot be made is refused with 409 and {"error": "nothing_to_settle" | "negative_balance" | "below_minimum"}, and everything stays pending for a later payout. Whatever a payout carried is never carried again. GET /admin/payouts returns {"payouts": [...]} in creation order and GET /admin/payouts/{id} one payout (404 {"error": "unknown_payout"}); the router needs to learn path parameters for that.

3. Reconciliation. GET /admin/reconciliation returns {"rows": [...]} with one row per provider/currency that has paid payments, ordered by provider then currency, each {provider, currency, grossCents (all paid payments), refundedCents, chargebackCents (lost disputes), feeCents (payment and dispute fees), netCents, settledCents (sum of payout totals), unsettledCents (what a payout run would total right now, whether or not it would be refused), disputeHoldCents (net of the payments held back by open disputes), openDisputeCents (sum of open disputes)}. These must always reconcile: netCents == grossCents - refundedCents - chargebackCents - feeCents == settledCents + unsettledCents + disputeHoldCents.

4. Command line. `php scripts/reconcile.php <scenario.json>` replays {"steps": [...]} against a fresh portal, where a step is {"op": "checkout", "sessionId", "cart"} | {"op": "event", "provider", "payload"} (signed for you) | {"op": "refund", "paymentReference", "amountCents"} | {"op": "payout", "provider", "currency"} | {"op": "get", "path"} (any GET route), and prints JSON {"steps": [{"op", "status", "body"}...], "reconciliation": [rows as above]}, the same JSON legacy/settled.exe prints for that scenario. An unreadable file, invalid scenario or unknown op prints "error: <message>" to stderr and exits 1; a missing argument exits 2.

Keep docs/ in step with the behaviour (state machine, webhook contracts, payment flow, and a note on settlement that records the rules you established).

5. Scale. The books are closed nightly for gateways that send tens of thousands of events a day: the portal holds about 40,000 orders, 28,000 payments, 3,000 refunds and 1,400 disputes at once. Everything above and every existing endpoint must stay correct and fast at that size. On a laptop, running one after the other and each starting from the state the previous ones leave, these workloads must finish within: 40,000 checkouts 6 s; 28,000 payment webhooks across the two gateways 8 s; 3,000 refunds by payment reference 4 s; 1,400 dispute webhooks 4 s; 10,000 replayed (duplicate) webhooks 4 s; the first payout for each gateway 6 s; the reconciliation report 5 s; GET /admin/payments with 40,000 orders 6 s; a second wave of payments and refunds followed by a payout 8 s; the disputes and payouts listings 3 s. Answers must not change. `python tests_visible/run_scale.py` replays a one-sixth size version of the same workload with proportional budgets and prints the timings (it checks amounts only for consistency).

The acceptance checks compare the portal with the reference on many scenarios, including unusual ones, and run the scale workload.
expected_behavior: Dispute webhooks open and close disputes, reduce or hold the payments they touch and drive the order state machine, answering like the reference engine.
Payouts settle each provider/currency stream with the reference engine's fees, dispute fees, holds, thresholds and line layout, and refuse empty, negative or too-small payouts.
The reconciliation report always satisfies net = gross - refunded - chargebacks - fees = settled + unsettled + dispute hold, with the reference engine's figures.
The router, refund endpoint and scripts/reconcile.php (including get steps) behave as described and match legacy/settled.exe; existing behaviour is unchanged.
The portal stays within the stated time budgets with tens of thousands of orders and payments without changing any answer.
